name: Python Basics
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Run Python scripts and the REPL, then use types, strings, input, if, loops, lists and functions, and read errors.

lesson.intro: Python reads almost like English, and you can run a line the moment you write it. This lesson takes you from your first script to small programs with numbers, text, decisions, loops, lists and functions, and teaches you to read error messages.
objectives: Run a script from the terminal and try ideas in the REPL
Predict the output of short programs with arithmetic, strings, if, loops and lists
Convert user input to numbers and format output with f-strings
Write small functions that take parameters and return values
Read a traceback to find the error type, the message and the failing line

sections.title: Running Python: scripts and the REPL
sections.key: A script runs top to bottom and shows only what you `print()`; the REPL runs one line at a time and echoes every value.
sections.body:
Save `print("Hello, Recurse!")` in `hello.py`, open a terminal in that folder and type `python3 hello.py`. That file is a **script**: Python code that runs from top to bottom, then exits. (On Windows the command is usually `python` or `py`.)

[[code]]

Type `python3` alone and you get the **REPL** (read, evaluate, print, loop) with a `>>>` prompt:

[[visual]]

A script runs one **statement** at a time. A variable exists only after the line that assigns it has run, and assigning again replaces the old value. Lines starting with `#` are comments.

Indentation is syntax: the indented lines under `if`, `for` or `def` form a block. Use four spaces per level.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: In the REPL
rows: Nothing: an assignment has no value to echo
Back to the terminal (Ctrl+Z, then Enter, on Windows)
visual.caption: In a script, a bare `2 + 3` is computed and thrown away: only `print()` shows output.

items.title: Syntax error
points: A missing colon or an unclosed quote
Found before anything runs: Python checks the whole file first

items.title: Runtime error
points: Such as using a name that does not exist yet (NameError)
Stops the program at that line
Every line above it has already run

sections.tip: Keep a REPL open next to your editor. When unsure what an expression does, type it in and look instead of guessing.
sections.pitfall: Typing `python3 hello.py` at the `>>>` prompt gives a SyntaxError. That command belongs in the terminal, so type `exit()` first.

activity.title: Read your first error
activity.prompt: Run it before changing anything. Notice that the first two lines print before the error: Python ran them, then stopped at the typo. Read the error message, fix the name and run it again.

print("total is", total)

check.question: A script prints start, then a line uses a misspelled variable name, then a line prints end. What do you see?
choices: Only the error, because Python checks every name before running
start and end, then the error
Nothing, because the file is rejected before it runs
check.explanation: A misspelled name is a runtime error (NameError), so Python only discovers it when it reaches that line. start has already printed and end never runs. Only syntax errors stop a file before anything runs.

sections.title: Values, types and arithmetic
sections.key: Every value has a type (int, float, str, bool); `/` always gives a float, `//` divides and rounds down, and `%` gives the remainder.
sections.body:
You need 7 eggs and they come in boxes of 6: `7 // 6` is 1 full box, and `7 % 6` says 1 egg is left over. Much everyday programming is arithmetic like this.

[[visual]]

`type(value)` tells you the type of anything, handy when a result surprises you.

[[visual 2]]

`//` and `%` work as a pair: `n % 2 == 0` tests for even, `n % 10` gives the last digit, and `minutes // 60` with `minutes % 60` splits minutes into hours and minutes.

Python follows math order, and parentheses cost nothing when in doubt:

[[visual 3]]

Mixing an int and a float gives a float. `0.1 + 0.2` prints `0.30000000000000004` in every language; Variables and Types explains why.

visual.title: Four types to start with
rows: Text in quotes: `'42'` is not a number

steps.label: Start
steps.note: `**` first (none here), then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%` left to right

sections.code:
print(type("42"))  # <class 'str'>
print(10 / 2)  # 5.0
print(7 // 2, 7 % 2)  # 3 1
print(-7 // 2)  # -4
print((2 + 3) * 4)  # 20

minutes = 135
print(minutes // 60, "h", minutes % 60, "min")
# 2 h 15 min
sections.pitfall: Expecting `/` to give a whole number. `9 / 3` is `3.0`, a float, and a float cannot be a list index. Use `//` when you need an int.

activity.title: Split seconds into hours, minutes and seconds
activity.prompt: Run it and look at the leftover seconds. Then apply // and % a second time, to what is left after the hours, to get minutes and seconds.

props.code:
total_seconds = 3725

hours = total_seconds // 3600
rest = total_seconds % 3600
print(hours, "hours and", rest, "seconds left over")
props.task: Make the program print exactly: 1 h 2 min 5 s

check.question: Which expression is True exactly when the int n is even?
check.explanation: % gives the remainder, and an even number leaves remainder 0 when divided by 2. n / 2 == 0 is only true when n is 0, and n // 2 == 0 is true for 0 and 1.

sections.title: Strings, slicing and f-strings
sections.key: Strings are immutable sequences: index from 0 (or -1 from the end), slice with `s[start:stop:step]` stopping before stop, and keep the new string each method returns.
sections.body:
A sign-up form hands you `"  ada lovelace "` and you want to show `Ada Lovelace`. Strings come with tools for exactly this cleanup.

A **string** is a sequence of characters, each with an **index** starting at 0. `len(s)` counts them.

[[visual]]

A **slice** `s[start:stop:step]` takes characters from start up to but not including stop. Slices forgive positions past the end (`"abc"[1:99]` is `'bc'`); plain indexing does not (`"abc"[5]` raises IndexError).

Strings are **immutable**: `s[0] = "J"` raises TypeError, and every method returns a new string. Chain them (`raw.strip().title()`) and keep the result.

[[visual 2]]

Join strings with `+` and repeat with `*` (`"ab" * 3` is `'ababab'`). To mix in numbers, use an **f-string**: `f"{name} owes ${price:.2f}"`. `:.2f` gives two decimals and `:,` adds thousands separators.

visual.title: String methods
rows: Removes spaces and newlines from both ends
Answer yes or no questions about the text

sections.code:
raw = "  ada lovelace "
clean = raw.strip().title()
print(clean)  # Ada Lovelace
print(len(raw), len(clean))  # 15 12

price = 3.5
print(f"{clean} owes ${price:.2f}")
# Ada Lovelace owes $3.50
print(f"{1234567:,}")  # 1,234,567
sections.pitfall: Calling a method and ignoring the result. `name.upper()` on a line by itself changes nothing, because strings never change in place. Write `name = name.upper()`.

activity.title: Clean and format a name
activity.prompt: Use strip() and title() to clean each part, then build the whole line with one f-string. Run after each change to see what each method does.

props.code:
first = "  grace "
last = "HOPPER"
year = 1906

print(first, last, year)
props.task: Make the program print exactly: Hopper, Grace (born 1906)

check.question: What does "python"[2:5] return?
check.explanation: Index 2 is t, and the slice stops before index 5, so you get t, h and o. 'thon' would need a stop of 6, and 'ytho' would start at index 1.

sections.title: Input, output and converting types
sections.key: `input()` always returns a string, so convert it with `int()` or `float()` before doing math, ideally on the same line you read it.
sections.body:
A tip calculator asks for the bill, the user types 40, and the program crashes with TypeError. `input(prompt)` shows the prompt and returns what the user typed as a `str`, even when it is all digits. Converting between types is called **casting**:

[[visual]]

Convert on the same line you read: `age = int(input("Age? "))`. Every later line then works with a real number.

`print()` takes any number of values, joins them with a space and ends with a newline. Change those with `sep=` and `end=`:

[[visual 2]]

The playground in this app cannot read the keyboard, so activities store a value in a variable as if the user had typed it.

visual.title: Casting
rows: `'42'`, needed to join a number onto text with `+`
`3`: drops the decimal part, no rounding
ValueError: not a whole number, so use `float()`
ValueError: bad input crashes at the cast

sections.code:
age = input("Age? ")  # the user types 20
print(type(age))  # <class 'str'>
next_year = int(age) + 1
print("Next year:", next_year)  # Next year: 21
sections.pitfall: Converting too late. If you write `age = input()` and convert in only one place, every other use of age is still a string. Convert once, right where you read it.

activity.title: Fix the bill splitter
activity.prompt: Run it and read the TypeError: you can't divide one string by another. Convert each value with the right function (the bill has a decimal point, the head count does not), then format the result to two decimal places.

props.code:
bill_text = "50.00"    # pretend the user typed this at input("Bill? ")
people_text = "3"      # and this at input("People? ")

share = bill_text / people_text
print(share)
props.task: Make the program print exactly: Each person pays $16.67

check.question: The user types 5 at n = input(). Which line prints 10?
check.explanation: n is the string '5', so int(n) * 2 is 10. n * 2, n + n and str(n) * 2 all give 55, because * repeats a string and + joins strings.

sections.title: Making decisions with if
sections.key: Python checks `if` and `elif` conditions top down and runs only the first true branch, so put the strictest condition first.
sections.body:
A store gives free shipping on orders of $50 or more, but only on weekends. Rules like that become `if` statements.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Combine conditions with `and` (both true), `or` (at least one) and `not` (flips). Chained comparisons read like math: `13 <= age <= 19` means `13 <= age and age <= 19`.

A classic trap: `if color == "red" or "blue":` is grouped as `(color == "red") or "blue"`, and a non-empty string is true, so the condition is always true. Write `color in ("red", "blue")`.

visual.title: An if chain

steps.label: `if score >= 90:`
steps.yes: Run the A block, skip the rest

steps.label: `elif score >= 80:`
steps.yes: Run the B block, skip the rest

steps.label: `elif score >= 70:`
steps.yes: Run the C block, skip the rest

steps.label: `else:`
steps.detail: Runs only when no condition was true

visual.caption: With score 85, only the B branch runs. Swap the first two conditions and a 95 would get a B.

visual.title: Comparisons
rows: Less than, at most, greater than, at least
Assignment, not comparison: `if x = 5:` is a SyntaxError

sections.code:
total = 62.0
day = "Sat"
if total >= 50 and day in ("Sat", "Sun"):
    print("Free weekend shipping")

answer = "Yes"
print(answer.lower() == "yes")  # True
sections.tip: Order elif branches from the strictest condition to the loosest, or an early branch will catch everything.
sections.pitfall: `if color == "red" or "blue":` is always true. Each side of `or` must be a complete comparison, or use `in` with a tuple of options.

check.question: If score were 95 in this example, which branches would run?
choices: The A, B and C branches
check.explanation: 95 >= 90 is true, so grade becomes A and Python skips every remaining elif and the else, even though 95 >= 80 is also true.

sections.title: Loops: for, range and while
sections.key: `for` runs once per item, `range()` stops before its stop value, and `while` repeats until its condition turns false, so something inside must change it.
sections.body:
Printing a times table, adding up prices, asking again until a password is right: loops do the repeating.

A `for` loop runs its block once for each item of a sequence: the characters of a string, the items of a list, or the numbers from `range()`.

[[visual]]

Most loops use the **accumulator** pattern: set a total (or count, or empty string) before the loop, update it inside, use it after. Starting it inside the loop resets it every pass.

A `while` loop checks its condition before each pass, so it may run zero times. If nothing ever makes the condition false, it is an **infinite loop** (Ctrl+C stops it).

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: range()
rows: 1 to 9: to include 10, the stop must be 11

items.title: for
points: You know what you loop over: each item, or n times

items.title: while
points: Loop until something changes, passes unknown in advance
Halving a number until it reaches 1, asking until the input is valid

sections.code:
total = 0  # accumulator, before the loop
for price in [4.5, 2.0, 3.5]:
    total += price  # total = total + price
print(total)  # 10.0

count = 3
while count > 0:
    print(count)  # 3, then 2, then 1
    count -= 1
print("liftoff")
sections.pitfall: Off-by-one errors: `range(1, 10)` stops at 9. To include 10, the stop must be 11.

check.question: What does list(range(5, 0, -2)) produce?
check.explanation: It starts at 5 and steps by -2, stopping before it reaches 0. So 5, 3 and 1 are produced; -1 is already past the stop value.

sections.title: Lists: storing many values
sections.key: A list holds many values in order and can change in place; `sorted()` returns a new list while `.sort()` sorts in place and returns None.
sections.body:
You have test scores for a whole class. One **list** holds them all in order: `scores = [77, 90, 85]`. Lists index and slice like strings, but they are **mutable**, so you can change them in place:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A list of 3 items has indexes 0, 1 and 2, so `scores[3]` raises IndexError: the classic off-by-one. Loop over the items directly with `for score in scores:` and you rarely need an index.

[[visual 3]]

A list can hold any type, even other lists, but it usually holds one kind of thing.

visual.title: List tools
rows: Adds one item to the end
Deletes the first item equal to 77
Removes and returns the last item
Work on a list of numbers

items.title: scores.sort()
points: Returns `None`, so `scores = scores.sort()` loses your list

sections.code:
scores = [77, 90, 85, 68]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print(f"Best {max(scores)}, average {average:.1f}")
# Best 90, average 80.0

for score in scores:
    if score < 70:
        print("Needs help:", score)  # 68
sections.pitfall: `scores = scores.sort()` sets scores to None. Either call `scores.sort()` on its own line or write `scores = sorted(scores)`.

activity.title: Summarize a week of temperatures
activity.prompt: Use max(), min(), sum() and len() on the list, and an f-string with :.1f for the average. Print one value per line.

props.task: Print exactly three lines: High: 27.5, then Low: 19.0, then Average: 23.2

check.question: nums = [3, 1, 2]. Which line leaves nums holding [1, 2, 3]?
check.explanation: sort() sorts the list in place. nums = nums.sort() replaces the list with None. sorted(nums) builds a sorted copy but throws it away because the result isn't stored, and lists have no sorted() method.

sections.title: Functions, and reading error messages
sections.key: `return` hands a value back to the caller; when code crashes, read the traceback bottom up: error type, failing line, then where the bad value came from.
sections.body:
You converted Celsius to Fahrenheit in four places and now find a bug in all four. A **function** lets you write those lines once and call them anywhere.

`def` gives a name, **parameters** in parentheses and an indented body. Calling it with **arguments** runs the body. `return` hands a value to the caller and ends the function; without one it returns `None`. Defining a function does not run it.

[[code]]

The last call crashes, and Python prints a **traceback**:

[[visual]]

The crash is on line 2, but the real mistake is on line 12, which passes the string `"20"`. Always ask where the bad value came from.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: The traceback
visual.caption: One entry per call, from your top-level code down to the line that failed. Python 3.11 and later also underline the failing part of the line.

visual.title: Errors you will meet most
rows: Not valid Python, such as `if x > 3` with no colon. Nothing runs
A name that does not exist yet, usually a typo: `print(totl)`
The wrong type (`"3" + 4`) or the wrong number of arguments (`greet()` with none)
The right type with a bad value: `int("abc")`

sections.code:
def fahrenheit(celsius):
    return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32


def show(celsius):
    print(f"{celsius} C is {fahrenheit(celsius)} F")


show(100)  # 100 C is 212.0 F
result = show(0)  # 0 C is 32.0 F
print(result)  # None: show returns nothing
show("20")  # line 12: crashes
sections.tip: Professional developers read tracebacks all day. Read them calmly: error type, failing line, then the value that was wrong.
sections.pitfall: Printing inside a function when the caller needs the value. The caller gets None, and the crash shows up far from the real mistake.

print(average([90, 85, 77]))
print(average([3, 4]))

check.question: A function prints its result but has no return statement. What does result = f() store in result?
choices: Nothing: the line raises an error
check.explanation: Every function call produces a value, and a function that finishes without return produces None. The printed text went to the screen, not to the caller.

keyTerms.definition: The interactive Python prompt (>>>) that reads a line, runs it, prints the result and waits for the next one.
A file of Python code, run with a command such as python3 file.py, that executes from top to bottom.
The kind of a value, such as int, float, str or bool, which decides what you can do with it.
The // operator: divide and round down to a whole number.
The % operator: the remainder after division, as in 7 % 3 == 1.
A piece of a sequence written s[start:stop:step]; the stop position is not included.
A string literal prefixed with f whose {expressions} are replaced by their values.
Converting a value to another type, for example int("42") or str(42).
An ordered, mutable collection written with square brackets, such as [77, 90, 85].
A variable set before a loop and updated on each pass, such as a running total.
The value a function hands back to its caller with return; None if there is no return.
The error report Python prints when a program crashes; read it from the bottom up.

summary: Run scripts with python3 file.py; only the REPL echoes values without print.
/ always gives a float, // rounds down and % gives the remainder.
Indexes start at 0, slices stop before their stop index, and string methods return new strings.
input() always returns a string, so cast with int() or float() before doing math.
Only the first true branch of an if chain runs, range() excludes its stop, and list.sort() returns None.
Functions hand values back with return; read tracebacks bottom up and ask where the bad value came from.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who has never programmed why int(input()) is needed before adding 1 to what the user typed, and how you would use the error message to find the problem if you forgot it.

questions.question: A script has five lines. Line 3 uses a variable name that was never assigned. What happens when you run it?
choices: Python skips line 3 and runs lines 4 and 5
Lines 1 and 2 run, then the program stops at line 3 with a NameError
Nothing runs, because Python checks every name before starting
All five lines run and the error is reported at the end
questions.explanation: Python executes lines in order and only discovers the missing name when it reaches line 3, so lines 1 and 2 have already run. Python checks syntax before starting, but not whether names exist, so the program does start.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
x = 5
x = x + 2
x = x * 10
print(x)
questions.explanation: Each line runs in order. x becomes 7, then 7 * 10 = 70. The right side is evaluated with the current value of x before the new value is stored.

questions.question: This script crashes on its first line. Why?
choices: print() can only display quoted strings, not variables
message is a reserved word in Python
message is used before the line that assigns it, so Python raises NameError
Variables must be declared with a type before use
questions.explanation: Python runs top to bottom, so when line 1 runs, message doesn't exist yet. Swap the two lines. Python never needs type declarations, and print() can show any variable.

questions.question: What does "recurse"[-3:] return?
questions.explanation: -3 is the third character from the end, 'r', and leaving out stop runs to the end, giving 'rse'. 'rec' would be [:3], the first three characters.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The slice starts at index 1 and takes every second character: indexes 1, 3 and 5, which are all 'a'. Leaving out stop means it runs to the end of the string.

questions.question: Complete the f-string so it prints Total: 4.50
questions.explanation: In an f-string the format goes after a colon, and .2f means two digits after the decimal point. :2f sets a minimum width of 2 instead and prints 4.500000. The other two options are syntax errors.

questions.question: This code should print Jane. What is wrong?
choices: Strings are immutable, so name[0] can't be assigned; build a new string such as "J" + name[1:]
The first character of a string is at index 1, not 0
Single characters must be written with single quotes
name must be converted with str() before indexing
questions.explanation: Python raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Strings can't change in place, so create a new one; name.capitalize() also works. Index 0 is valid and refers to the first character.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: + joins two strings, giving '34', and adds two ints, giving 7. print separates its two values with a space. There is no TypeError because each + has the same type on both sides.

questions.question: The user types 21. Why does this crash?
choices: if statements can't compare against a number literal
age is the string '21', and comparing a string with an int raises TypeError; use int(input(...))
input() returns None until the user presses Enter twice
questions.explanation: input() always returns a string, and Python refuses to order a str against an int, so it raises TypeError. Convert first: age = int(input("Age? ")). Parentheses around a condition are optional.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: int("12") is 12. int(3.9) drops the decimal part instead of rounding, giving 3. So the total is 15, not 16.

questions.question: What happens when Python runs int("3.5")?
questions.explanation: int() only parses text that looks like a whole number, and '3.5' doesn't, so it raises ValueError. int(3.5) with a float works and returns 3; for the string, use int(float("3.5")).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Python runs only the first branch whose condition is true. 25 > 10 is checked first, so it prints warm and skips the elif, even though 25 > 20 is also true. Checking temp > 20 first would fix the order.
questions.concept: only the first true branch runs

questions.question: Complete the condition so it prints teen only for ages 13 to 19.
questions.explanation: Both conditions must be true, which is what and means. With or, every age passes, because every number is either at least 13 or at most 19. && is not Python syntax. 13 <= age <= 19 would also work.

questions.question: Complete the condition so it checks whether guess equals secret.
questions.code:
secret = 7
guess = 7
if guess _____ secret:
    print("correct")
questions.explanation: == compares two values. A single = assigns, and inside an if condition it is a SyntaxError. === exists in JavaScript, not Python.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total += n
print(total)
questions.explanation: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3 and 4 and stops before 5, so the total is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. If you got 15, you included the stop value.

questions.question: This program never prints done. What is wrong?
choices: while loops can't use the < operator
print(count) must come after the loop
count should start at 1 instead of 0
count never changes, so count < 3 stays true forever; add count += 1 inside the loop
questions.explanation: The loop prints 0 over and over because nothing updates count. Adding count += 1 inside the loop makes the condition false after three passes. Starting at 1 would still loop forever.

questions.question: When would you choose a for loop, and when a while loop?
questions.answer: Use a for loop when you know what you are iterating over, such as a list, a string or range(n). Use a while loop when you repeat until a condition changes and can't know the number of passes in advance, such as asking again until the input is valid.
questions.explanation: A for loop steps through the items for you. A while loop relies on you to update its condition, which is why forgetting that update causes an infinite loop.

questions.question: In the REPL, typing 2 + 3 shows 5. What does a script containing only the line 2 + 3 show when you run it?
choices: Nothing: a script only shows what you print
A SyntaxError, because the line has no print
questions.explanation: The REPL echoes the value of every expression you type, but a script calculates 2 + 3 and throws the result away. A bare expression is valid Python, so there's no error. In scripts, use print(2 + 3).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: // divides and rounds down, giving 3. % gives the remainder, 1, because 7 = 2 * 3 + 1. print separates the two values with a space.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: / always produces a float, even when the division is exact, so the result is 5.0. Use 10 // 2 when you need the int 5.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: // and * have the same precedence and run left to right: 17 // 5 is 3, and 3 * 5 is 15. % also binds tighter than +, so 17 % 5 is 2, and 15 + 2 is 17. This always holds: (n // d) * d + n % d gives back n.

questions.question: Match each value to its type.
questions.explanation: Quotes make a value a string, even when it looks like a number. A decimal point makes a float. True and False, capitalized, are the two bool values.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: lower() returns "oh, hello otto", which has four o's: one in oh, one in hello and two in otto. count is case sensitive, so msg.count("o") without lower() would give only 1.

questions.question: Complete the code so it prints ADA LOVELACE.
questions.explanation: upper() makes every letter uppercase. title() gives Ada Lovelace and capitalize() gives Ada lovelace. Python strings have no uppercase() method, so that raises AttributeError.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: end="" replaces the usual newline with nothing, so the second print continues on the same line. sep="-" puts a dash between y and z instead of a space.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Python reads the condition as (color == "red") or "blue". The comparison is False, so or returns "blue", and a non-empty string counts as true. The fix is color in ("red", "blue").

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
n = 10
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)
questions.explanation: n goes 10, 5, 2, 1. That is three passes; after the third, n is 1 and n > 1 is false, so the loop stops. Writing down n and steps after each pass is the reliable way to trace a while loop.
